n: The final week begins. Near Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem, Jesus sends two disciples ahead on an errand.

f.g: A small village on the Mount of Olives; the name means “house of unripe figs.”
A ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley, with a view over the temple.

n: He tells them they’ll find a donkey tied up with her colt, and to bring both. Jesus knows exactly what they will find.

f.g: Opposite you, just ahead.

f.w: an ass tied, and a colt with her

n: If anyone objects, they need only say “The Lord needs them,” and the owner will send them.

f.g: ought = anything.

n: Matthew explains that this happened to fulfill prophecy.
Quoting Zechariah: Zion’s King comes humbly on a donkey. Kings rode warhorses to battle but donkeys in peace; Jesus comes as a king of peace.

f.g: Sion = Zion; a poetic name for Jerusalem and its people.

f.w: Behold, thy King cometh unto thee

n: The disciples obey exactly.
They bring the animals and lay their cloaks on them as a saddle, and Jesus sits on them.

f.g: Spreading cloaks was a sign of royal honor.

n: The crowd spreads cloaks and branches on the road — a red-carpet welcome for a king. John says palm branches, giving us “Palm Sunday.”

f.g: strawed = strewed, scattered.

n: Crowds shout “Hosanna” and words from Psalm 118, a psalm sung at Passover. They openly hail Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of David.

f.g: Hebrew “Save, we pray!” — it became a shout of praise.

n: The whole city is stirred, asking “Who is this?” — the question Matthew’s Gospel has been answering all along.

f.g: moved = stirred up, shaken, like an earthquake (Greek seiō).

n: The crowd answers that he is the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.
Jesus drives the merchants and moneychangers out of the temple courts. Their business, in the court open to Gentiles, had turned worship into commerce.

f.g: They exchanged pilgrims’ coins for the approved currency used to pay the temple tax, often at a profit.
Doves were the sacrifice of the poor.

n: He quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah: God’s house is meant for prayer, but they’ve made it a hideout for robbers.

f.w: My house shall be called the house of prayer

n: With the commerce cleared away, the blind and the lame — once excluded from parts of the temple — come to Jesus, and he heals them.
The chief priests and scribes are furious at his miracles and at children shouting praise to the Son of David in the temple.

f.g: Greatly indignant.
The high priest and leading priestly families who controlled the temple.

n: Jesus answers with Psalm 8: God has ordained praise from the mouths of children. The children see what the leaders miss.

f.w: Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings

f.g: Nursing infants.

n: Jesus spends the night in Bethany, about two miles away, likely with Mary, Martha, and Lazarus.

f.g: A village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives.
Stayed overnight.

n: Returning to the city the next morning, Jesus is hungry.

f.g: A reminder of his real humanity.

n: He finds a fig tree full of leaves but no fruit, and curses it; it withers. It acts out a parable about religion that looks good but bears no fruit.

f.g: Fig trees with leaves usually showed early fruit buds as well.
presently = immediately.

n: The disciples are amazed at how fast it withered.

f.g: How quickly.

n: Jesus turns the moment into a lesson on faith: faith without doubt can do even greater things, like moving a mountain into the sea.

f.w: If ye have faith, and doubt not

n: Whatever they ask in prayer, believing, they will receive — prayer offered in faith and in harmony with God’s will.
In the temple the leaders challenge Jesus: by what authority does he act — cleansing the temple and teaching there?

f.w: By what authority doest thou these things?

f.g: Lay leaders who sat with the priests on the Sanhedrin council.

n: Jesus responds, as rabbis often did, with a question of his own.

f.w: I also will ask you one thing
f.g: Answering a question with a question was a common rabbinic teaching method.

n: Was John’s baptism from God or from men? They realize that if they say “from heaven,” Jesus will ask why they didn’t believe John.

f.g: whence = from where.
“Heaven” was a respectful way of saying “God.”

n: But if they say “from men,” the crowd, who revere John as a prophet, will turn on them.

f.w: all hold John as a prophet

n: So they dodge with “We don’t know.” Since they won’t answer honestly, Jesus declines to answer them. The answer is implied: his authority, like John’s, comes from God.

f.g: We don’t know — an evasive answer.

n: Jesus tells a parable: a father asks his first son to work in the vineyard that day.
The son refuses, but later changes his mind and goes.

f.g: repented = changed his mind and turned around.

n: The second son politely agrees — then never goes.

f.w: I go, sir: and went not

n: Which son obeyed? The first. Jesus says tax collectors and prostitutes, who repented, are entering God’s kingdom ahead of these religious leaders.

f.g: Which of the two.
harlots = prostitutes.

n: Notorious sinners believed John and repented; the leaders saw that change and still refused to believe.
Another parable, drawn from Isaiah’s Song of the Vineyard: an owner plants a vineyard with every care and rents it to tenant farmers.

f.g: husbandmen = tenant farmers.
A watchtower for guarding the crop.

n: At harvest he sends servants to collect his share of the fruit.

f.g: The owner’s rightful portion of the crop.

n: The tenants beat, kill, and stone his servants — a picture of how Israel often treated the prophets.
He sends more servants, and they are treated the same way.

f.g: A larger group of servants.

n: Finally he sends his own son, sure they’ll respect him — a clear reference to Jesus himself.

f.g: reverence = respect.

n: The tenants see the heir and plot to kill him to seize the inheritance.
They throw him out of the vineyard and kill him — foreshadowing Jesus’s death outside Jerusalem’s walls.

f.w: cast him out of the vineyard

n: Jesus asks his listeners what the owner will do when he comes.

f.g: The owner.

n: The leaders answer, condemning themselves: he will destroy the wicked tenants and rent the vineyard to others who will give him its fruit.

f.w: render him the fruits in their seasons
f.g: render = give, pay.

n: Jesus quotes Psalm 118: the stone the builders threw away has become the cornerstone. He is that rejected stone.

f.w: The stone which the builders rejected

f.g: The cornerstone or capstone — the most important stone in the building.

n: The kingdom will be taken from those who reject him and given to a people who produce its fruit.

f.w: given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof

n: The stone image continues: those who stumble over Christ will be broken, and those on whom his judgment falls will be crushed.

f.w: whosoever shall fall on this stone

n: The chief priests and Pharisees realize the parables are about them.

f.w: they perceived that he spake of them

n: They want to arrest him on the spot but fear the crowds, who regard Jesus as a prophet.

f.w: they took him for a prophet
